items.stem: Which term describes a return to the basic or fundamental principles of a religion, often in response to modern change?
items.answer: Fundamentalism
items.markingKey: Fundamentalism: a return to the basic or fundamental principles of a religion, often in response to modern change. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “cosmopolitanism”, and give one example.
items.answer: An outlook that embraces diversity, tolerance and openness to change. Example: accepting different lifestyles and beliefs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (an outlook that embraces diversity, tolerance and openness to change); 1 mark for a relevant example such as accepting different lifestyles and beliefs. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “literalism” and “fundamentalism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Literalism: interpreting sacred texts as the literal, unchanging word of God (e.g. reading creation stories as historical fact). Fundamentalism: a return to the basic or fundamental principles of a religion, often in response to modern change (e.g. calls for strict application of sacred law).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A religious movement near Muscat uses social media to call for a return to “pure” traditions, opposes women working outside the home and denounces Western films and music. Suggest how a Weberian sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Weberian theory: fundamentalism arises when traditional groups perceive threats to their values from social change (Bruce).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A conservative religious group in Dhaka campaigns for schools to teach the literal truth of sacred texts and to ban books it considers immoral. Explain how a Weberian sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: fundamentalism arises when traditional groups perceive threats to their values from social change (Bruce).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying how fundamentalist groups use online media.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how fundamentalist groups use online media but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Distinguish between “project identity” and “New Christian Right”.
items.answer: Project identity: Castells’s term for a forward-looking identity that engages with social movements. New Christian Right: a politically and morally conservative Protestant movement in the USA.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “resistance identity” and “New Christian Right”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Resistance identity: Castells’s term for a defensive identity formed in reaction to globalisation (e.g. a group rejecting Western values to defend its traditions). New Christian Right: a politically and morally conservative Protestant movement in the USA (e.g. campaigns against abortion and same-sex marriage).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how fundamentalist groups use online media. Explain one limitation of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how fundamentalist groups use online media. [2]

items.stem: A conservative religious group in Seoul campaigns for schools to teach the literal truth of sacred texts and to ban books it considers immoral. Compare how late modern and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Late modernity: fundamentalism is a defensive response to the uncertainty and choice of late modernity and globalisation (Giddens). Marxism: fundamentalism grows from poverty, inequality and the effects of global capitalism, offering the oppressed an alternative identity.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Arjun analysed a survey of 600 adults in rural and urban areas. Table: adults agreeing (%) | Rural residents | Urban residents. Sacred texts should be read literally | 46% | 35%. Religious law should guide national law | 40% | 31%. Globalisation threatens our values | 50% | 45%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Rural residents and Urban residents for Sacred texts should be read literally. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that fundamentalism is a reaction to globalisation.
items.answer: (a) 35 − 46 = -11 percentage points (Urban residents compared with Rural residents). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Urban residents than for Rural residents among Sacred texts should be read literally, Religious law should guide national law, Globalisation threatens our values; Globalisation threatens our values had the highest figure for Urban residents. Urban areas are more cosmopolitan (Giddens). Qualifications: Agreement does not mean support for fundamentalist movements; urban residents also agree in large numbers; question wording; correlation is not causation. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 600 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 46 and 35; 1 mark for 11 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “cyber-religion”, and give one example.
items.answer: Religion practised or organised online. Example: online prayer groups and virtual worship.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (religion practised or organised online); 1 mark for a relevant example such as online prayer groups and virtual worship. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “deterritorialisation” and “cyber-religion”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Deterritorialisation: the separation of religion from particular places (e.g. a faith community connected online across countries). Cyber-religion: religion practised or organised online (e.g. online prayer groups and virtual worship).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A megachurch in Istanbul holds services with rock music and coffee shops, broadcasts worldwide online and sells branded books and clothing. Suggest how a Weberian sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religious ideas can bring about social change; beliefs such as the Protestant ethic shaped economic behaviour, and religion can motivate social movements (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Mei, in Riyadh, joins a live-streamed prayer meeting from a church in another country, follows a Buddhist teacher on social media and attends a local mosque’s open day. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: religion is ideology that legitimates class inequality and offers false comfort to the oppressed (“the opium of the people”), creating false consciousness (Marx, Lenin).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the content of religious websites. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable; it is cheap and the sources (newspapers, television, websites) are easy to obtain. Limitations: coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree; it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the content of religious websites but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “deterritorialisation”.

items.stem: What is the difference between “deterritorialisation” and “televangelism”?
items.answer: Deterritorialisation: the separation of religion from particular places. Televangelism: the use of television and other media to spread religious messages.

items.stem: Explain Helland’s argument that the internet has created religion online and online religion, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Helland distinguished top-down religion online from more democratic online religion. Criticism: Most online religious activity supplements rather than replaces offline participation.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Postmodernism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.answer: 1. Counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. 2. It shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the content of religious websites. [4]

items.stem: Two surveys, each of 500 adults in Santiago, produced the results below. Table: adults in the last month (%) | 2015 | 2023. Watched a religious service online | 9% | 26%. Used a prayer or meditation app | 3% | 10%. Followed a religious leader on social media | 10% | 22%. (a) Calculate the gap between Used a prayer or meditation app and Watched a religious service online in 2015 and in 2023, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that religion is adapting to globalisation and new media.
items.answer: (a) 2015: 6 percentage points; 2023: 16 percentage points; the gap widened. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Watched a religious service online, Used a prayer or meditation app, Followed a religious leader on social media; Watched a religious service online had the highest figure for 2023. Online religion increased during health emergencies. Qualifications: Online activity may supplement rather than replace attendance; most adults do not take part; self-report; growth may be temporary. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 500 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (6 and 16); 1 mark for “widened”. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful structured interviews are for studying the content of religious websites.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the content of religious websites but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: After a terrorist attack, some newspapers in Bogotá describe it as part of a “war between civilisations”, while interfaith groups hold joint vigils. Compare how postmodernist and neo-Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religious identities are fluid and hybrid; global conflict is not simply between fixed religious blocs. Neo-Marxism: the clash of civilisations is an ideology that creates enemies and justifies Western power (Said).

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying how members of religious communities view each other in a divided city.
items.answer: Strengths: every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how members of religious communities view each other in a divided city but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).

items.stem: A conservative religious group in Manila campaigns for schools to teach the literal truth of sacred texts and to ban books it considers immoral. Explain how a Weberian sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: fundamentalism arises when traditional groups perceive threats to their values from social change (Bruce).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how fundamentalist groups use online media. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it is cheap and the sources (newspapers, television, websites) are easy to obtain; it allows representations to be compared over time or between different media. Limitations: it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it; counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how fundamentalist groups use online media but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Zara analysed a survey of 600 adults in rural and urban areas. Table: adults agreeing (%) | Rural residents | Urban residents. Sacred texts should be read literally | 55% | 40%. Religious law should guide national law | 44% | 27%. Globalisation threatens our values | 50% | 39%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Rural residents and Urban residents for Globalisation threatens our values. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of attitudes to religion and change. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that fundamentalism is a reaction to globalisation.
items.answer: (a) 39 − 50 = -11 percentage points (Urban residents compared with Rural residents). (b) Respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Urban residents than for Rural residents among Sacred texts should be read literally, Religious law should guide national law, Globalisation threatens our values; Sacred texts should be read literally had the highest figure for Urban residents. Urban areas are more cosmopolitan (Giddens). Qualifications: Agreement does not mean support for fundamentalist movements; urban residents also agree in large numbers; question wording; correlation is not causation. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 600 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 50 and 39; 1 mark for 11 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the use of television and other media to spread religious messages?
items.answer: Televangelism
items.markingKey: Televangelism: the use of television and other media to spread religious messages. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “televangelism”?
items.answer: The use of television and other media to spread religious messages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the use of television and other media to spread religious messages. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “deterritorialisation” and “televangelism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Deterritorialisation: the separation of religion from particular places (e.g. a faith community connected online across countries). Televangelism: the use of television and other media to spread religious messages (e.g. preachers broadcasting to millions).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A megachurch in Dhaka holds services with rock music and coffee shops, broadcasts worldwide online and sells branded books and clothing. Suggest how a religious market sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Religious market theory: religion is a market: when there is competition and choice, religious organisations meet people’s needs and religiosity stays strong (Stark and Bainbridge).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Two surveys, each of 500 adults in Nairobi, produced the results below. Table: adults in the last month (%) | 2015 | 2023. Watched a religious service online | 9% | 28%. Used a prayer or meditation app | 8% | 15%. Followed a religious leader on social media | 12% | 18%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Followed a religious leader on social media change between 2015 and 2023?
items.answer: +6 percentage points
items.markingKey: 18 − 12 = +6 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Freya compared surveys of 800 adults in Cape Town about online religious activity. Table: adults in the last month (%) | 2015 | 2023. Watched a religious service online | 6% | 26%. Used a prayer or meditation app | 4% | 14%. Followed a religious leader on social media | 14% | 21%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for 2023. (b) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Watched a religious service online between 2015 and 2023. Show your working. (c) Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires to collect data like these.
items.answer: (a) Watched a religious service online (26%). (b) (26 − 6) ÷ 6 × 100 = 333.3%. (c) They measure what people say they do, not what they actually do.
items.markingKey: (a) Watched a religious service online, 26%. [1] (b) 1 mark for (26 − 6) ÷ 6 × 100; 1 mark for 333.3% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (c) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2]

items.stem: Yusuf compared surveys of 200 adults in Dubai about online religious activity. Table: adults in the last month (%) | 2015 | 2023. Watched a religious service online | 8% | 26%. Used a prayer or meditation app | 8% | 14%. Followed a religious leader on social media | 10% | 19%. (a) Calculate the gap between Watched a religious service online and Used a prayer or meditation app in 2015 and in 2023, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that religion is adapting to globalisation and new media.
items.answer: (a) 2015: 0 percentage points; 2023: 12 percentage points; the gap widened. (b) Respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Watched a religious service online, Used a prayer or meditation app, Followed a religious leader on social media; Watched a religious service online had the highest figure for 2023. The internet allows religion to be practised anywhere. Qualifications: Online activity may supplement rather than replace attendance; most adults do not take part; self-report; growth may be temporary. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 200 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (0 and 12); 1 mark for “widened”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes conflict between groups within or between religions?
items.answer: Sectarian conflict
items.markingKey: Sectarian conflict: conflict between groups within or between religions. [1]

items.stem: Outline what Huntington meant by arguing that conflicts between civilisations, defined largely by religion, will dominate global politics.
items.answer: Huntington argued that globalisation makes religious identities more important and that the West faces conflict with other civilisations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Huntington argued that globalisation makes religious identities more important and that the West faces conflict with other civilisations. [2]

items.stem: Jones argued that religion is rarely the only cause of conflict; it often overlaps with ethnicity, nationalism and economic interests. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Jones argued Huntington ignores divisions within religions and the political causes of conflict. Criticism: Religious identity can still intensify conflicts.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Weberian theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A content analysis of 200 articles about a conflict in two newspapers in Muscat produced the results below. Table: articles mentioning each (%) | Newspaper X | Newspaper Y. Religion named as the main cause | 58% | 41%. Economic or political causes named | 32% | 50%. Interfaith cooperation mentioned | 9% | 16%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Newspaper X and Newspaper Y for Religion named as the main cause (Newspaper Y minus Newspaper X)?
items.answer: -17 percentage points
items.markingKey: 41 − 58 = -17 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Lucas analysed 400 newspaper articles about a regional conflict. Table: articles mentioning each (%) | Newspaper X | Newspaper Y. Religion named as the main cause | 59% | 39%. Economic or political causes named | 32% | 52%. Interfaith cooperation mentioned | 9% | 13%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Newspaper X and Newspaper Y for Interfaith cooperation mentioned. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the media exaggerate the role of religion in conflict.
items.answer: (a) 13 − 9 = +4 percentage points (Newspaper Y compared with Newspaper X). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Newspaper Y than for Newspaper X among Economic or political causes named, Interfaith cooperation mentioned; the figure is lower for Newspaper Y than for Newspaper X among Religion named as the main cause; Economic or political causes named had the highest figure for Newspaper Y. News values favour conflict over cooperation. Qualifications: Content analysis does not show the real causes of the conflict; categories overlap; two newspapers may not be typical. The data also come from content analysis of 400 articles in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 9 and 13; 1 mark for 4 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]
